items.title: Bug0 Releases QA Agent to Automate Regression Testing With Cached Playwright Replays
items.summary:
QA Agent is a new source-available Playwright library for agentic browser regression testing. The agent associates test instructions expressed in natural language to actions on the user interface, caches those when appropriate for faster CI replays, remapping them to test specifications when the user interface changes. Verification is based on multi-model consensus and vision model evaluations.

By Bruno Couriol

items.title: Browser Use in Managed Deep Agents
items.summary: Managed Deep Agents now runs a browser for your agent, with tools tuned for context-efficient browser use and a handoff so you can sign in yourself.
items.story_key: story|title:browser use in managed deep agents
items.content_excerpt: Agents have gotten good enough to work where we work, and a lot of that work happens in a browser. Booking travel, canceling a subscription, or filing a claim all happen on sites built for people clicking through pages, including ones the agent didn't plan to visit. Often there's no API an agent can call. Fetching the page with curl doesn't get far either, since it returns the HTML before any JavaScript renders the page and can't click anything. Personal agents like Instinct and Meta's Muse already work this way. Browser agent traffic is growing fast too, and DataDome saw agentic browser requests jump 4.7x in September alone. Managed Deep Agents lets you build and deploy agents in LangSmith without running any infrastructure. You write the agent's instructions and tools, and LangSmith runs the harness and runtime. Today, we're giving these agents a browser, so you can build your own agents that work on the web. Managed Deep Agents runs the browser too, and gives your agent tools tuned for it. In this post, we cover where a browser helps and how to turn it on, including handing the browser to a person when the agent needs one. Then we walk through how it works under the hood. Agents built with open source Deep Agents can use a browser too . We'll cover how we tested and tuned the browser tools in a deep dive next week. With a browser and tools to drive it, an agent can read what renders on a page and click through it, the same way you (a human) would. The browser stops after idle_ttl_seconds without activity (10 minutes by default), so you don't pay for a browser nobody is using. Some steps still need a person, and signing in is the most common one. You don't want to give the agent your password, where it would end up in the model's messages, in traces, and with a model provider. So when the agent hits a login page, it calls browser_handoff with a reason, like "Please sign in to Acme Travel so I can continue." In LangSmith Studio , the UI where you chat with and debug your agent, you get an interactive card with the same browser. You sign in yourself, click Hand back , and the agent picks up where it left off, already signed in. Handoff comes with every managed browser and works automatically in Managed Deep Agents channels like Slack, so there's nothing extra to set up. This matters most with scope="user" . items.title: Can Frontier Models See Past a Decoy? Elorian Tests Visual Reasoning
items.summary: A new decoy counting benchmark exposes a gap between seeing and reasoning. Elorian’s Glimpse tries to bridge it by thinking with images.
items.story_key: story|title:can frontier models see past a decoy elorian tests visual reasoning

Author matches published credits. Year applies to posts; wiki entries have no author or publication year. You can also use author:"Ada" or type:podcast in non-regex searches. A new decoy counting benchmark exposes a gap between seeing and reasoning. Elorian’s Glimpse tries to bridge it by thinking with images. This month Elorian launched its first visual reasoning model , Glimpse . It’s being promoted as “a new category of visual thinking model: a system that reasons about the physical world from what it sees.” So how does Glimpse compare to both frontier models and world models in vision tests? A new benchmark called DecoyCount , co-released by Elorian, provides some answers. We quizzed CEO Andrew Dai on the benchmark, and also talked about Elorian’s positioning in a crowded models landscape. Elorian emerged from stealth in April with $55 million in seed funding , co-led by Striker Venture Partners, Menlo Ventures and Altimeter Capital. Now, in partnership with AI data company Mercor , Elorian is announcing the DecoyCount benchmark, which tests whether language models genuinely count objects or rely on visual shortcuts and substitution heuristics. According to a paper accompanying the release , frontier models scored below 50% accuracy on DecoyCount — the highest was GPT-6 Astra, with 43.17%. Elorian’s new model isn’t mentioned in the paper, but Dai told us that Glimpse scored 50.48% in an internal test. Regarding the frontier models, the paper concludes that “stronger general reasoning does not by itself generalize to aligned visual reasoning.” How the benchmark works: “DecoyCount exposes interpretable counting failures across seven mechanisms.” To make sure it was a like-for-like comparison with the frontier models, we asked whether the paper’s evaluation images were withheld from Glimpse’s training? “The evaluation images and text were withheld from our training, and our contamination check found no overlap in the training data checked,” Dai replied, via email. “Without any cues, Glimpse scored 50.48% on the 1,660 DecoyCount items, making it the only model in the comparison to clear 50%. The closest was GPT-6 Astra at 43.17%, about 7 points behind, and Gemini-3.8-flash scored 32.71% while Qwen3.8-max scored 28.31%, and Claude-Fable-5.1 came in at 25.22%.” Dai did note that Glimpse’s results “come from

items.title: Day 0 support for Mistral Large 4 on vLLM
items.summary: Day-0 vLLM support for Mistral Large 4 with sparse MLA, cross-layer KV sharing, DSpark speculative decoding, DCP/PCP long context and NIXL P/D on NVIDIA Blackwell.
items.story_key: model:mistral|variant:large|title:day 0 support for mistral large 4 on vllm
items.content_excerpt: We're excited to announce day-0 support for Mistral Large 4 in vLLM. Mistral Large 4 is Mistral's new frontier mixture-of-experts native multimodal model. It combines a DeepSeek-style sparse attention stack (MLA plus a DSA top-k indexer) with several new architecture features: cross-layer KV sharing, NoPE layers, SSMax and LeRoPE. It ships with a built-in DSpark speculative decoding drafter and a Pixtral vision encoder. Supporting it took more than a model file. ML4 runs on vLLM's model runner V2 (MRV2) with breakable CUDA graphs. Its building blocks live in a new vllm/models/mistral/ package, and the work produced generic improvements to decode context parallelism (DCP), prefill context parallelism (PCP), DSpark, NIXL-based disaggregated serving and HiSparse host-memory KV offload. Mistral Large 4 support ships in the vllm/vllm-openai:mistral-large-4 Docker image, which also includes mistral-common 1.13. The commands below run vllm serve inside it: NVFP4 does not trade quality for speed. On multimodal, long-context, agentic coding, business automation and cyber evals it stays within 2.1 points of FP8 on every task, and the mean difference is −0.3 points. Token consumption is matched too: mean completion tokens stay within about 4% of FP8. It is also faster and lighter: at TP8, NVFP4 decodes 1.08–1.19x faster per token than FP8 without spec decoding (1.18–1.22x with DSpark) and holds ~1.5x the KV cache. Long context (DCP). Add --decode-context-parallel-size 8 to shard the latent KV cache across the 8 ranks. It requires the default FP8 KV cache. Multimodal. Pass --limit-mm-per-prompt '{"image": N}' to allow up to N images per prompt. For multi-node, disaggregated P/D and other tested configurations, see the Mistral Large 4 recipe . Sparse MLA + DSA indexer. ML4 reuses vLLM's sparse-MLA stack (FlashMLA sparse with the fp8_ds_mla latent cache, plus the sparse indexer with an FP8 indexer cache). ML4-specific differences are layered on top: shared-indexer layers that reuse the top-k of the nearest earlier indexer layer, an indexer with its own SSMax, and NoPE indexers on NoPE layers. Per token, the KV cache stores 47,136 bytes: 41,328 for the MLA latent and 5,808 for the indexer. Cross-layer KV sharing. Nine NoPE layers read the latent KV written by layer 35 instead of writing their own. We added kv_sharing_target_layer_name to MLAAttention and AttentionLayerBase . items.title: Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face
items.story_key: model:mistral|variant:large|title:welcome le chonk mistral large 4 on hugging face
items.content_excerpt: Mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about 1T total, 49B active parameter , and a context window of 1M tokens . There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team. It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings). Mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more! Mistral Large 4 combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a Pixtral vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions. Mistral Large 4 scores 82% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index test that asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch the software. Mistral reports that several closed frontier models score near zero on the same test because they refuse to attempt the work. This is super important for defenders, because fixing a vulnerability usually requires reproducing the vulnerability. In Mistral’s internal testing, Mistral Large 4 was also useful for malware analysis, vulnerability prioritisation and writing detection rules, which the model was not explicitly trained for. Mistral mainly positions the model for defensive security work. Vulnerability research and incident response often appear like attacks in model input, so closed source filters can block them. A team that depends on an API can also lose access in the middle of an incident. Crucially, open weight models put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. That said, the model still declines harmful requests: on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, its average refusal rate is higher than any other open weight model. For community builders, an open weight model like Mistral Large 4 unlocks a load of downstream use cases. You could build your own cyber system around your code base, crash logs, and malware samples. items.title: Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms
items.story_key: story|variant:speech|title:introducing anyspeechrecognizer and anydecisionmodel open models for speech and
items.content_excerpt: Language models can do a lot. They write, summarize, translate, and call tools. But they're only a small part of what machine learning can do. Say a customer calls your support line. First, you want to know what they said (speech recognition). Then, you want to decide where to send them (decision). You could hand both to a language model, but there are models built for each that are better, faster, and less expensive. In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap , we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift. With AnyLanguageModel and swift-huggingface now on their 1.x releases, we're extending the same approach to speech and decisions: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of model. Both packages can download open models from the Hugging Face Hub and run them on device. Computers have been transcribing speech for decades, and in the past few years, they've gotten very good at it. Apple platforms already have an API for it. macOS 26 and iOS 26 introduced SpeechAnalyzer , Apple's new speech-to-text API. You add modules such as SpeechTranscriber and SpeechDetector to an analyzer, give it a file or a stream of audio buffers, and read results from async sequences as they arrive. AssetInventory installs the models, so your app decides when downloads happen. It's a well-designed API, but the only engine behind it is Apple's. AnySpeechRecognizer keeps the API and lets you choose the engine: The package mirrors SpeechAnalyzer , SpeechTranscriber , DictationTranscriber , SpeechDetector , and AssetInventory , with Apple's Speech framework as the default engine. If your code uses that shared API, changing the import is enough. To use Parakeet instead, change only how you create the transcriber: The steps for installing assets, running the analyzer, and reading results stay the same. The README has a complete example and lists the differences from Apple's framework. Parakeet v3 is NVIDIA's Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3 . It's a polyglot: it recognizes 25 European languages and works out which one it's hearing, so you don't pass a locale. Parakeet Ultra is Moondream's post-trained take on v3 . It was more accurate in most of our measurements. All three Parakeets run on the package's own Core ML runtime, which supports file and live input, volatile results, word timing, and word confidence. Qwen3-ASR is Alibaba's speech model, in 0.6B and 1.7B sizes. It recognizes 30 languages and 22 Chinese dialects, including Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, and Korean, which Parakeet doesn't cover.

items.title: Smarter cost controls for serverless
items.summary: At Databricks, our serverless compute usage has grown more than 3x in the past year,...
items.story_key: story|title:smarter cost controls for serverless
items.content_excerpt: At Databricks, our serverless compute usage has grown more than 3x in the past year, and thousands of customers now run mission critical notebooks, jobs, and pipelines on it. As adoption climbs, the question every platform team asks first only gets louder: how do we gain better visibility into serverless costs and keep the cost within our budget? Databricks customers running serverless SQL and Model Serving already attribute spend, govern access, and monitor consumption without touching a single cluster knob. We are now bringing that same functionality to serverless compute for notebooks, jobs, and pipelines. We are making serverless cost controls work the way platform teams already expect it to. On classic compute, cost control lived in the infrastructure. You capped spend by capping machines: node counts, instance types, autoscaling ranges, and cluster policies that fenced in what users could provision. The controls were required because you had to manage the infrastructure on your own. Serverless takes those knobs away, on purpose. Provisioning, scaling, and right-sizing infrastructure is the platform's burden now, handled by Databricks, which is a big part of the value. But cost control has to live somewhere, so it moves up a layer. Instead of attaching to machines, it attaches to people and workloads. Who is allowed to run serverless, how fast a workload is allowed to spend, and where the cost lands are the questions that matter now. Classic compute answered these with three tools: tags to attribute cost, entitlements to control access, and cluster size limits to cap spend. Serverless needs the same three. Two of them exist today, and the third is coming. Attribution starts with tags. On classic compute you tagged the cluster; on serverless you tag the compute, and every DBU that compute runs carries that tag through to billing. The same table answers the audit question you will want before you change anyone's access: who is actually running serverless today, and how much are they spending? That is one more query, ranked by consumption, and the full examples live in the system tables documentation. Availability: Serverless Compute tags for attribution is currently available in Beta . Observability is already available and customers can already monitor serverless cost with system tables on AWS , Azure , and Google Cloud . items.title: PerceptRL: Making Visual Perception Rewardable in MLLMs from Answers to Interactions
items.summary: Fine-grained visual perception remains a bottleneck during post-training of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), as perceptual errors can constrain gains from reasoning-focused optimization. Although image-caption pre-training improves perception, its influence can weaken as subsequent stages change data mixtures and objectives. Continuing caption supervision during post-training is challenging because subjective, information-dense descriptions complicate verifiable reward design. We present PerceptRL, which strengthens perception at two complementary levels. Perception RL uses a multi-agent pipeline to extract verified errors from dense image captions and convert the corresponding visual facts into QA pairs with fixed answer labels and rule-based rewards. Chain QA links correlated errors, while multiple-choice QA combines unrelated errors. A specialized route targets high-error domains with tailored verification, and a domain-agnostic general route covers errors beyond these domains. Perception Agentic RL addresses fine-grained and dense cases unresolved by single-turn Perception RL through multi-turn inspection with visual tools. We observe coordinate drift even in models trained to use tools, where incorrect crops or annotations distort evidence and propagate errors. Coordinate Injection corrects spatial operations in cold-start trajectories, while a grounding-aware process reward supervises intermediate spatial fidelity alongside final-answer correctness. Training proceeds through shared cold-start SFT, single-turn Perception RL, and multi-turn Perception Agentic RL. Across seven benchmarks under a shared tool-use protocol, PerceptRL achieves 71.6% average accuracy, surpassing the base model with the same tools and the strongest evaluated frontier VLM by 15.7 and 5.2 percentage points, respectively.

items.title: Where Should the Evaluation Budget Go in LLM-Driven Agent Scaffold Evolution?
items.summary: Large language model (LLM)-driven agent scaffold evolution improves agent workflows through iterative candidate generation and evaluation. Evaluation both guides subsequent search and determines the final scaffold, but evaluating every candidate on the full task set incurs substantial execution costs. We investigate how evaluation budgets can be allocated across these two roles. Our experiments show that sparse feedback can sustain productive evolution, while additional targeted evaluation improves final selection. Replay analyses further show that shared informative items and a common scoring reference support comparisons among closely matched candidates. Motivated by these findings, we propose \method, an evaluation allocation framework that combines sparse search-time feedback with targeted final confirmation. A short fully evaluated warm-up establishes a shared informative core and calibrates a response model whose item parameters remain fixed during search. After search, \method refits the model and applies paired successive halving, reusing accumulated observations and executing only missing evaluations. Across four benchmarks and two evolution frameworks, \method achieves higher mean performance than full evaluation in most settings while using approximately half as many evaluation cells.

items.title: DocSkill: Skill-Integrated Agentic Reasoning for Multilingual Multi-Hop Document Question Answering
items.summary: Multilingual multi-hop document question answering (MMHop-DocQA) requires locating and integrating evidence across complex layouts, document pages, and diverse languages. Existing approaches include single-pass processing and adaptive tool use, but learning to coordinate evidence acquisition, cross-page integration, and answer verification remains challenging. To address this challenge, we present DocSkill, an agentic framework with a learned skill-orchestration policy for adaptive evidence acquisition and reasoning. The policy selects, revisits, or skips skills according to the evolving evidence state. To construct supervision for skill orchestration, bounded Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) explores alternative skill trajectories offline. These trajectories provide demonstrations for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and preference pairs for Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). We further introduce MMHop-DocBench, a multilingual multi-hop document QA dataset with training and test splits, containing 60K QA pairs across 10 languages and eight document domains. Its HopGen pipeline builds hierarchical page-element graphs to derive traceable cross-page evidence paths and generate grounded QA pairs with page- and element-level evidence annotations. Experiments show that DocSkill with Qwen3-VL-8B achieves 41.0 accuracy and 49.2 F1 on MMHop-DocBench, exceeding the strongest evaluated baseline by 5.5 and 6.3 points, respectively, and achieving competitive performance on MMLongBench-Doc and DocBench.

items.title: claude-code v2.1.310
items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added the Monitor tool and plugin monitors on Bedrock, Vertex, and Foundry, and when telemetry or nonessential traffic is disabled; long foreground sleeps are now blocked there too
  • Fixed requests failing behind some gateways and compatible servers that reject the effort-2025-11-24 beta value or mid-conversation system messages; Claude Code now retries without them
  • Fixed background cleanup deleting some recent files, such as pasted images, when cleanupPeriodDays is set to a very large value
  • Fixed compaction after a "Prompt is too long" error keeping too much of a conversation with dense text, such as base64 or SVG, so the next request could fail again
  • Fixed file read permission prompts not showing where a symbolic link leads
  • Fixed a question's auto-continue timeout firing the moment the external editor closed after a long edit
  • Windows: Fixed PreToolUse and PermissionRequest hooks letting a tool call through when Git Bash is missing and the hook's command is only quoted strings, such as a quoted path
  • Improved auto mode's prompt before the first read outside the working directories: it now says when blocking those reads makes shell commands ask for permission
  • Improved memory use of non-interactive sessions (-p, Agent SDK) during compaction when the transcript file is very large
  • Improved a mod's Image to draw inside tmux with allow-passthrough and focus-events on, in kitty, Ghostty, and iTerm2 3.5+ with fullscreen rendering, where it showed only its alt text
  • Linux: Improved /sandbox and the sandbox startup warning to name Ubuntu's AppArmor restriction on user namespaces, and how to lift it, when it keeps bubblewrap from starting the sandbox
  • Changed the error for an MCP tool call that times out in a non-interactive session while the server's elicitation is unanswered: it now tells Claude that no answer came and not to repeat the call
  • [VSCode] Fixed pressing Enter on the plan review card's "Send feedback and keep planning" button approving the plan instead of sending your comments back
  • [VSCode] Fixed the panel showing "Something went wrong" after "Switch branch & continue" on a cloud session opened from Session history's Web tab
  • [Cloud sessions] Added Claude Code cloud sessions and Remote Control permissions to Enterprise custom roles, so Owners can control access to each by role
  • [Cloud sessions] Added a Choose file button to load a cloud environment's setup script from a file
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed failed saves and archives in the cloud environment edit dialog showing no error inside the dialog
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed failed routine API token actions showing only a toast; the error now appears in the routine edit dialog
  • [Cloud sessions] Improved the session start checklist to show a cloud environment's setup script output in a scrolling box
  • [Cloud sessions] Changed turning on Cloud sessions or Remote Control in admin settings to ask for confirmation and list the custom roles that have that permission
  • [Cloud sessions] Changed the cloud environment dialog to open network access, setup script and environment variables from rows instead of listing every editor at once
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude Tag treating ! commands such as !restart and !help as ordinary messages when sent in bold, italic or strikethrough
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude Tag admin channel and workspace pages being replaced by a load error when a background refresh of the bundle list fails
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude Tag's spend limits page in admin settings reporting that no channels match a filter while channel names are still loading
  • [Code Review] Fixed the Code Review admin section hiding its repositories and switches after a failed refresh of the repository list
  • [Code Review] Improved the Code Review admin section to retry the first load and show one Try again banner when it still fails
